title: Top 50 JavaScript Interview Questions (Basic to Advanced & Coding)
subtitle: Comprehensive Q&A and coding problem bank with self-assessment checks for complete interview preparation

chapters.title: Complete Interview Questions & Answer Bank
chapters.summary: Full collection of 50 JavaScript interview questions ranging from core fundamentals and coding challenges to advanced engine internals.

sections.title: Q1: What are the primitive data types in JavaScript vs objects?
sections.content: JavaScript has 7 primitive data types: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `symbol`, and `null`. Primitives are immutable and passed by value. Objects (including arrays, functions, and plain objects) are mutable collections of key-value properties and are passed by reference.
keyTakeaways: Primitive types are immutable and stored directly by value.
Objects are mutable reference types stored by memory location.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does typeof null return in JavaScript?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Due to a historical bug retained for backward compatibility, `typeof null` evaluates to `'object'`.

sections.title: Q2: What is the difference between var, let, and const?
sections.content: `var` is function-scoped (or globally scoped) and hoisted with an initial value of `undefined`. `let` and `const` are block-scoped and hoisted into a Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ). `const` creates a read-only variable reference that cannot be reassigned after declaration.
keyTakeaways: `var` is function-scoped; `let` and `const` are block-scoped.
`let` and `const` exist in the Temporal Dead Zone prior to declaration.

interactiveQuiz.question: What error occurs when accessing a let variable before its declaration line?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Accessing a `let` or `const` variable inside its Temporal Dead Zone throws a `ReferenceError`.

sections.title: Q3: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
sections.content: `==` (loose equality) performs type coercion to convert operands to a common type before comparing. `===` (strict equality) checks for equality without type conversion; both the value and the type must match.
keyTakeaways: `==` converts operands to the same type before comparison.
`===` compares both value and data type without coercion.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the result of the comparison: [] == false?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: An empty array `[]` coerces to `''`, which coerces to numeric `0`, matching `false` coerced to `0`.

sections.title: Q4: How does Hoisting work in JavaScript?
sections.content: Hoisting is JavaScript's behavior of moving variable and function declarations to the top of their containing scope during creation phase. Function declarations are hoisted with their complete definitions, `var` declarations are hoisted with `undefined`, while `let` and `const` remain uninitialized in the TDZ.
keyTakeaways: Function declarations are hoisted with their definitions fully accessible.
`var` is hoisted as `undefined`; `let`/`const` are placed in the TDZ.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is printed when calling foo() declared as: var foo = function() { return 1; }; before assignment?
options: TypeError: foo is not a function
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `var foo` is hoisted initialized as `undefined`. Calling `undefined()` raises a `TypeError`.

sections.title: Q5: What is Scope and the Scope Chain?
sections.content: Scope determines the accessibility of variables in code. JavaScript has Global Scope, Function Scope, and Block Scope. When a variable is referenced, JavaScript looks in the current scope; if not found, it traverses up the Scope Chain to outer enclosing scopes until it reaches the global scope.
keyTakeaways: Lexical scope means inner scopes can access outer scope variables.
The scope chain lookup travels outward up to global scope.

interactiveQuiz.question: Where does lexical scope determine variable accessibility from?
options: The location where functions are called
The location where functions/variables are defined in source code
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Lexical scope is determined statically at code authoring time based on block/function structure.

sections.title: Q6: What is a Closure in JavaScript?
sections.content: A closure is the combination of a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment. Closures give inner functions access to an outer function's scope variables even after the outer function has finished executing.
keyTakeaways: Functions retain references to variables in their lexical environment.
Powers state encapsulation, module patterns, and memoization.

interactiveQuiz.question: What will console.log print: for(var i=0; i<3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); }?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Because `var` is function-scoped, all timeouts close over the same single `i` variable whose final value is 3.

sections.title: Q7 [Coding]: Implement a counter function using closures that supports increment, decrement, and getValue.
keyTakeaways: Enables private variables without native class private fields.
Exposes object methods that maintain access to closed-over state.

interactiveQuiz.question: Can code outside createCounter access or modify the internal count variable directly?
options: No, it is private inside the closure scope
Yes, if count is converted to string
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `count` is enclosed strictly inside the function scope and cannot be mutated except via exposed closure methods.

sections.title: Q8: How does the `this` keyword work in different execution contexts?
sections.content: The value of `this` depends on how a function is called: standard method call (`obj.fn()`) sets `this` to `obj`; plain function call sets `this` to `window`/`undefined` (strict mode); constructors (`new Fn()`) bind `this` to the new instance; arrow functions bind `this` lexically from their outer scope.
keyTakeaways: Standard function `this` is bound dynamically at call time.
Arrow function `this` is determined statically from lexical outer scope.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is `this` inside an arrow function defined within an object method?
options: The object instance containing the outer method
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Arrow functions do not bind their own `this`; they inherit `this` lexically from the enclosing method.

sections.title: Q9: What is the difference between call(), apply(), and bind()?
sections.content: `call()` invokes a function with a specified `this` context and arguments passed individually (`fn.call(ctx, arg1, arg2)`). `apply()` invokes the function with arguments passed as an array (`fn.apply(ctx, [arg1, arg2])`). `bind()` returns a new function with `this` bound permanently.
keyTakeaways: `call` accepts arguments comma-separated; `apply` accepts an array.
`bind` returns a bound copy of the function without immediate execution.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which method executes a function immediately with an array of arguments?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `apply()` accepts an array of arguments and executes the target function immediately.

sections.title: Q10: How does Prototypal Inheritance work in JavaScript?
sections.content: Objects in JavaScript have an internal `[[Prototype]]` link (exposed as `__proto__`). When accessing a property on an object, JavaScript looks at the object first, then traverses up the prototype chain until the property is found or `null` is reached.
keyTakeaways: Objects inherit properties and methods dynamically via prototype delegation.
Top of the prototype chain ends at `Object.prototype.__proto__ === null`.

interactiveQuiz.question: What method creates a new object using an existing object as its prototype?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `Object.create(proto)` initializes a new object whose `[[Prototype]]` points directly to `proto`.

sections.title: Q11: How do ES6 Classes relate to Prototypal Inheritance?
sections.content: ES6 Classes are syntactic sugar built on top of prototypal inheritance. Class methods are stored on the constructor's `prototype` property, and the `extends` keyword establishes prototype inheritance between prototype objects.
keyTakeaways: Classes provide cleaner syntax over function prototypes.
Under the hood, classes use prototypal delegation and function constructors.

interactiveQuiz.question: Where are methods defined inside an ES6 class body attached?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Methods defined in a class body are placed on `Class.prototype` to be shared efficiently across instances.

sections.title: Q12: How do Arrow Functions differ from Regular Functions?
sections.content: Arrow functions: 1) Do not bind their own `this` or `arguments` object. 2) Cannot be used as constructor functions with `new`. 3) Do not have a `prototype` property. 4) Cannot be used as generator functions.
keyTakeaways: Arrow functions inherit lexical `this` and `arguments`.
They cannot act as constructors or generators.

interactiveQuiz.question: What error is thrown when invoking an arrow function with the `new` keyword?
options: TypeError: Arrow function is not a constructor
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Arrow functions lack internal `[[Construct]]` methods and throw a `TypeError` when instantiated with `new`.

sections.title: Q13: What is the JavaScript Event Loop?
sections.content: The Event Loop enables non-blocking asynchronous execution. JavaScript executes synchronous code on the single Call Stack. Asynchronous tasks offload to APIs and queue callbacks into the Microtask Queue (Promises) or Macrotask Queue (timers). The Event Loop empties the call stack, drains all microtasks, and then processes one macrotask.
keyTakeaways: Call stack processes synchronous tasks sequentially.
Microtasks (Promises) take execution priority over Macrotasks (setTimeout).

interactiveQuiz.question: Which queue has higher execution priority: Microtask or Macrotask Queue?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The Event Loop clears the complete Microtask Queue before executing the next Macrotask.

sections.title: Q14 [Coding]: Predict the execution output of this asynchronous code snippet.
keyTakeaways: Synchronous code runs to completion first.
Microtasks (`Promise`) run before Macrotasks (`setTimeout`).

interactiveQuiz.question: In what order are the microtask and macrotask logged above?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `3` is a Promise microtask and executes prior to timer macrotask `2`.

sections.title: Q15: What is a Promise and what are its three states?
sections.content: A Promise represents the eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation. Its states are: 1) `pending` (initial state), 2) `fulfilled` (operation succeeded), 3) `rejected` (operation failed). State transitions are immutable once settled.
keyTakeaways: Promises encapsulate async outcomes in pending, fulfilled, or rejected states.
Transitions are permanent; settled states cannot change.

interactiveQuiz.question: What occurs if resolve() and reject() are both called inside the same Promise executor?
options: First settled call determines final state; subsequent calls are ignored
interactiveQuiz.explanation: A Promise can only settle once. Whichever settlement function executes first permanently locks state.

sections.title: Q16: How does async/await work under the hood?
sections.content: `async/await` is syntactic sugar over Promises and Generators. An `async` function always returns a Promise. When `await` is encountered, function execution yields pause control back to the Event Loop until the awaited Promise settles.
keyTakeaways: `async` functions wrap return values in resolved Promises.
`await` pauses async function execution without blocking the main event thread.

interactiveQuiz.question: What does an async function return if it explicitly returns a plain primitive value 42?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `async` functions automatically wrap return values into resolved Promise instances.

sections.title: Q17: What is the difference between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race, and Promise.any?
sections.content:
- `Promise.all()`: Resolves when all resolve; rejects immediately if any reject.
- `Promise.allSettled()`: Resolves when all settle (fulfilled or rejected).
- `Promise.race()`: Settles as soon as any promise settles.
- `Promise.any()`: Resolves as soon as any promise fulfills; rejects if all reject.
keyTakeaways: `Promise.all` fails fast on initial rejection.
`Promise.allSettled` guarantees tracking outcome states for every promise.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which Promise combinator rejects ONLY if ALL input promises reject?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `Promise.any` resolves on the first successful fulfillment and rejects only when all inputs reject.

sections.title: Q18 [Coding]: Implement a simple polyfill for Promise.all().
keyTakeaways: Tracks completed promise counts against total length.
Preserves array output index placement matching original input ordering.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is results[index] = val used instead of results.push(val) in Promise.all polyfills?
options: To maintain correct original promise ordering regardless of completion speed
Because push is forbidden inside promises
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Async promises resolve in arbitrary order. Direct index placement guarantees output matches input sequence.

sections.title: Q19: What is Event Bubbling and Event Capturing in the DOM?
sections.content: DOM event propagation has 3 phases: 1) **Capturing Phase** (event travels down from document root to target), 2) **Target Phase** (event reaches target node), 3) **Bubbling Phase** (event bubbles up from target to document root). `addEventListener` defaults to handling events in the bubbling phase.
keyTakeaways: Capturing travels downward; Bubbling travels upward.
Passing `{ capture: true }` attaches listeners to capturing phase.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which method stops an event from propagating further up or down the DOM tree?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `stopPropagation()` prevents the event from bubbling up or capturing further along the DOM path.

sections.title: Q20: What is Event Delegation and why is it useful?
sections.content: Event Delegation is a pattern where a single event listener is attached to a parent element to manage events for all its present and future child elements by leveraging event bubbling and checking `event.target`.
keyTakeaways: Reduces memory overhead by minimizing total event listener count.
Handles dynamically inserted child elements without requiring new listener attachments.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which event property points to the actual element that triggered the event?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `event.target` refers to the target element that initiated the event.

sections.title: Q21 [Coding]: Write a debounce function implementation.
keyTakeaways: Resets timer on every new event trigger call.
Ideal for search auto-complete inputs and window resize handlers.

interactiveQuiz.question: When does a debounced function execute after rapid continuous triggers?
options: At fixed interval ticks during events
Only after events pause for the specified delay duration
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Debouncing waits for continuous event bursts to stop for `delay` milliseconds before firing once.

sections.title: Q22 [Coding]: Write a throttle function implementation.
keyTakeaways: Executes function at regular, rate-limited time intervals.
Ideal for scroll position tracking and window resize listeners.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does throttling differ from debouncing?
options: Throttling runs code on worker threads
Throttling guarantees periodic execution during continuous triggers
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Throttling executes calls periodically at set intervals; debouncing postpones execution until events pause.

sections.title: Q23: What is the difference between a Shallow Copy and a Deep Copy?
sections.content: A shallow copy (`Object.assign()`, `{...obj}`) copies top-level properties, but nested objects/arrays retain memory references. A deep copy (`structuredClone()`, `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())`) recursively duplicates all nested structures, creating completely independent object graphs.
keyTakeaways: Shallow copy leaves nested objects linked by reference.
Deep copy duplicates all nested layers independently.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which modern native JavaScript global function performs deep copying safely?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `structuredClone()` is the modern native JS API for deep cloning complex values (including Maps, Sets, and Date).

sections.title: Q24 [Coding]: Write a function to recursively flatten a deeply nested array.
keyTakeaways: Uses recursion and `Array.isArray()` to unravel nested sub-arrays.
Native equivalent: `arr.flat(Infinity)`.

interactiveQuiz.question: What built-in Array prototype method flattens nested arrays to any depth directly?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `arr.flat(Infinity)` recursively flattens nested sub-arrays to a single flat array.

sections.title: Q25: What is the difference between ES Modules (ESM) and CommonJS (CJS)?
sections.content: CommonJS (`require`/`module.exports`) is synchronous and evaluated dynamically at runtime. ES Modules (`import`/`export`) are asynchronous, statically analyzed at compile-time (enabling tree-shaking), and strict mode by default.
keyTakeaways: CJS loads modules dynamically at runtime using `require()`.
ESM uses static `import/export` syntax allowing build optimization and tree-shaking.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why does ES Module syntax enable Tree-Shaking optimization in bundlers?
options: Because ESM runs on thread pools
Because ESM imports/exports are statically structure-analyzed before execution
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Static `import/export` structure lets bundlers detect and remove unused exports during compilation.

sections.title: Q26: What is Function Currying?
sections.content: Currying is a technique of transforming a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument (`f(a, b, c)` into `f(a)(b)(c)`).
keyTakeaways: Transforms multi-argument functions into unary function chains.
Enables partial application and higher-order functional composition.

interactiveQuiz.question: How would you call a curried function add(a)(b) to calculate 2 + 3?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Curried functions accept single arguments sequentially through chained function calls: `add(2)(3)`.

sections.title: Q27 [Coding]: Implement a generic curry() helper function.
keyTakeaways: Compares gathered `args.length` against the expected function parameter count (`fn.length`).
Recursively returns outer wrapper functions until all parameters are fulfilled.

interactiveQuiz.question: What property of a Function object indicates its declared expected argument count?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `fn.length` exposes the number of formal parameters expected by the function definition.

sections.title: Q28: What is the difference between Map, Set, WeakMap, and WeakSet?
sections.content:
- `Map`: Key-value store accepting any data type key.
- `Set`: Collection of unique values.
- `WeakMap` / `WeakSet`: Hold garbage-collectable **weak references** strictly to objects/symbols. Their keys/elements are non-enumerable.
keyTakeaways: `Map` supports keys of any type; `WeakMap` keys MUST be objects/symbols.
`WeakMap` references do not prevent garbage collection if no other references exist.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why are WeakMap keys non-enumerable?
options: Because keys can be garbage collected at any non-deterministic time
Because keys are stored on disk
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Since keys can be garbage collected asynchronously, iteration over WeakMap keys is non-deterministic and forbidden.

sections.title: Q29: What are Symbols in JavaScript and what are their primary use cases?
sections.content: `Symbol` is a primitive type that returns guaranteed unique identifiers (`Symbol('id') !== Symbol('id')`). They are used to create private object property keys that avoid key collision issues across external modules.
keyTakeaways: Symbols generate guaranteed unique primitive property keys.
Used for well-known metaprogramming symbols (e.g., `Symbol.iterator`).

interactiveQuiz.question: Do Symbol object keys appear in standard for...in loops or Object.keys()?
options: No, they are skipped by standard iterations
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Symbol keys are ignored by standard iterations; retrieve them via `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols()`.

sections.title: Q30: How do Generators and Iterators work in JavaScript?
sections.content: An Iterator is an object with a `next()` method returning `{ value, done }`. Generators (`function*`) are special functions that can pause execution using `yield` and resume when `next()` is called on their returned Generator object.
keyTakeaways: `yield` pauses generator functions and returns execution values.
Generators implement the iterable protocol automatically.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which keyword pauses execution inside a Generator function?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `yield` keyword yields control back to caller and pauses generator execution.

sections.title: Q31: What are Proxy and Reflect objects in JavaScript?
sections.content: A `Proxy` object wraps a target object and intercepts fundamental operations (like property lookup, assignment, enumeration, function invocation) using trap handlers. `Reflect` provides built-in methods to perform default underlying JavaScript operations.
keyTakeaways: Proxies enable metaprogramming by trapping object operations.
Used heavily in reactivity systems (like Vue 3 reactivity).

interactiveQuiz.question: Which Proxy trap intercepts property read access (e.g., obj.prop)?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `get` trap intercepts property read operations on proxied target objects.

sections.title: Q32: What is Strict Mode ('use strict') and what changes does it enforce?
sections.content: Strict Mode enforces cleaner JavaScript execution rules: 1) Prevents accidental global variable creation. 2) Throws errors on silent fails (read-only writes). 3) Disables `with` statements. 4) Sets default `this` in plain functions to `undefined`.
keyTakeaways: Opt-in via `'use strict';` directive.
Transforms silent runtime errors into explicit thrown exceptions.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the value of `this` inside a standard plain function call in Strict Mode?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Strict mode sets `this` to `undefined` in un-bound plain function calls.

sections.title: Q33: How does Memory Management and Garbage Collection work in V8?
sections.content: JavaScript automatically manages memory using Mark-and-Sweep garbage collection algorithm. Roots (global variables, call stack references) are traversed. Any allocated memory object unreachable from roots during mark phase is swept and freed.
keyTakeaways: V8 uses Mark-and-Sweep garbage collection algorithm.
Unreachable objects disconnected from root scope are marked for memory deallocation.

interactiveQuiz.question: What memory condition causes an object to be reclaimed during garbage collection?
options: When the object is unreachable from active roots
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Objects unreachable via reference paths starting from root nodes are swept as garbage.

sections.title: Q34 [Coding]: Implement a generic memoize() utility function.
keyTakeaways: Caches calculation results using serialized stringified arguments as keys.
Avoids duplicate costly computations on identical input arguments.

interactiveQuiz.question: What trade-off does memoization introduce into applications?
options: Higher CPU usage for lower RAM
Higher Memory (RAM) usage to save Computation (CPU) time
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Memoization trades increased memory storage space to avoid repeated computation time.

sections.title: Q35: What is MutationObserver and when should it be used?
sections.content: `MutationObserver` is a built-in API that provides the ability to watch for changes made to the DOM tree (child additions/removals, attribute mutations, text content modifications) asynchronously without performance polling.
keyTakeaways: Asynchronously monitors DOM tree mutations.
Replaces legacy performance-heavy DOM mutation events.

interactiveQuiz.question: How are DOM mutation notifications delivered by MutationObserver?
options: Synchronously inside the main thread frame
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `MutationObserver` callbacks fire asynchronously as microtasks before browser repaints.

sections.title: Q36: What are Web Workers and how do they communicate with the main thread?
sections.content: Web Workers allow running background JavaScript scripts in parallel threads separate from the main execution thread. Communication occurs via message passing using `worker.postMessage()` and `onmessage` event handlers.
keyTakeaways: Runs heavy scripts in isolated background threads without UI thread blocking.
Workers lack direct access to DOM objects (`document`, `window`).

interactiveQuiz.question: Can a standard Dedicated Web Worker directly manipulate DOM nodes using document.getElementById?
options: No, workers do not have access to the DOM
Yes, if imported via ES modules
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Web Workers operate in isolated thread scopes without access to the DOM or `window` object.

sections.title: Q37 [Coding]: Write a custom polyfill for Array.prototype.map().
keyTakeaways: Iterates over input array elements and constructs a new mapped array.
Handles sparse array indices using `i in this` checks.

interactiveQuiz.question: Does Array.prototype.map() mutate the original calling array instance?
options: No, it returns a new array instance
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `map()` is a pure non-mutating transformation method that returns a brand new array.

sections.title: Q38 [Coding]: Write a custom polyfill for Array.prototype.reduce().
keyTakeaways: Initializes accumulator to `initialValue` or array element index 0.
Sequentially processes callback updates across array elements.

interactiveQuiz.question: What occurs if myReduce is called on an empty array without an initialValue parameter?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Calling `reduce()` on an empty array without supplying an initial value throws a `TypeError`.

sections.title: Q39: What is requestAnimationFrame() and why is it preferred over setInterval for animations?
sections.content: `requestAnimationFrame(cb)` instructs the browser to execute a specified callback before the next repaint frame (typically 60fps/120fps). It synchronizes with hardware display refresh rates and pauses execution in inactive background tabs to conserve power.
keyTakeaways: Synchronizes animation updates directly with screen repaint frames.
Pauses automatically in hidden background browser tabs.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is requestAnimationFrame superior to setInterval(fn, 16) for smooth CSS/Canvas animations?
options: Matches screen refresh rates and pauses when tab is hidden
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `requestAnimationFrame` aligns frame steps with monitor refresh rate and reduces resource usage when backgrounded.

sections.title: Q40: What is Tail Call Optimization (TCO)?
sections.content: Tail Call Optimization occurs when a recursive function call is the final execution statement inside a function. The engine reuses the current stack frame instead of allocating new stack frames, preventing stack overflow errors on infinite recursion.
keyTakeaways: Reuses call stack frame when recursion occurs at tail position.
Prevents `Maximum call stack size exceeded` errors on deep recursions.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which requirement must be met for a function to qualify for Tail Call Optimization?
options: The recursive call must be the absolute final execution statement in the function
interactiveQuiz.explanation: TCO requires that the function return value be directly the output of the recursive call without remaining outer frame operations.

sections.title: Q41 [Coding]: Write a deepEqual function to compare two objects deeply.
keyTakeaways: Compares primitives via `===` and recursively inspects nested object keys.
Validates key count matching prior to recursive nested property checks.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the return value of deepEqual({a: 1, b: {c: 2}}, {a: 1, b: {c: 2}})?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Both objects possess identical keys and structural primitive values across all nested layers.

sections.title: Q42: What are Service Workers and Progressive Web Apps (PWAs)?
sections.content: A Service Worker is an event-driven worker registered between client browsers and network backends. It intercepts network requests (`fetch` event), manages offline application caches (`CacheStorage`), and powers push notifications for PWAs.
keyTakeaways: Acts as a programmable network proxy client-side.
Enables offline capability and background data sync.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which network event is intercepted by Service Workers to serve offline cached assets?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Service Workers listen to the `fetch` event to intercept outgoing network calls and serve cached responses.

sections.title: Q43: What triggers a CORS Preflight OPTIONS request in browsers?
sections.content: A preflight `OPTIONS` request is sent automatically by browsers prior to cross-origin requests if: 1) Method is NOT `GET`, `HEAD`, or `POST`. 2) Custom HTTP headers (like `Authorization`) are included. 3) `Content-Type` is not simple (`application/json`).
keyTakeaways: Preflight verifies cross-origin permissions using HTTP `OPTIONS` requests.
Triggered by non-simple headers or non-simple Content-Type values.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which Content-Type triggers a CORS preflight request when sent in a POST request?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `application/json` is classified as a non-simple MIME type, triggering an automated preflight request.

sections.title: Q44: What are the Time Complexities (Big O) of common Array operations?
sections.content:
- `push()` / `pop()`: $O(1)$ (end of array).
- `unshift()` / `shift()`: $O(n)$ (requires re-indexing elements).
- `indexOf()` / `includes()`: $O(n)$ linear search.
- `sort()`: $O(n \log n)$ average time complexity.
keyTakeaways: Adding/removing from start (`shift`/`unshift`) is $O(n)$.
Array access by numeric index (`arr[i]`) is $O(1)$.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is array.unshift() an O(n) operation whereas array.push() is O(1)?
options: Because unshift allocates memory on disk
Because unshift requires re-indexing every existing array element index
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Inserting an element at index 0 requires shifting all existing $n$ elements forward by 1 index.

sections.title: Q45: How do V8 Hidden Classes (Shapes) optimize property access speed?
sections.content: V8 assigns Hidden Classes (Shapes) to objects. When objects share identical key property structures and declaration order, V8 reuses the same Hidden Class, enabling fast memory offset property lookups instead of dictionary hash lookups.
keyTakeaways: Instantiate object properties in consistent order to reuse V8 shapes.
Avoid deleting properties (`delete obj.prop`) to prevent downgrading to slow dictionary mode.

interactiveQuiz.question: How should you nullify an object key without invalidating its V8 Hidden Class shape?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Assigning `undefined` or `null` maintains object structure, preserving V8 hidden class optimizations.

sections.title: Q46 [Coding]: Write a function to flatten a deeply nested object using dot notation keys.
keyTakeaways: Uses recursion to append nested keys into dot-separated paths.
Ignores primitive key value properties while drilling into child object trees.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the flattened key output for { user: { address: { city: 'Paris' } } }?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Nested object traversal joins property names using dot notation into `'user.address.city'`.

sections.title: Q47: What are common causes of Memory Leaks in client-side JavaScript?
sections.content: 1) **Accidental global variables** (`window.leakedVar = ...`). 2) **Forgotten timers or callbacks** (`setInterval` retaining closed variables). 3) **Out-of-DOM references** (holding references to removed DOM nodes in JS arrays). 4) **Uncleared Event Listeners**.
keyTakeaways: Always clear timers (`clearInterval`) and detach unused event listeners.
Remove JS variable references pointing to detached DOM nodes.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which situation leads to a Detached DOM Tree memory leak?
options: Removing a DOM node from document while retaining a reference to it inside a JS variable
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If a detached node is referenced in JS, GC cannot sweep the node or its child subtree from memory.

sections.title: Q48 [Coding]: Make a custom object iterable using Symbol.iterator.
keyTakeaways: Implementing `[Symbol.iterator]` enables `for...of` loops and spread syntax (`[...obj]`).
Iterator methods return objects conforming to `{ value, done }` contracts.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which built-in loop syntax consumes objects that implement the Symbol.iterator interface?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: The `for...of` loop is specifically designed to consume objects implementing the iterable protocol.

sections.title: Q49: What is Tree Shaking and how does static analysis make it possible?
sections.content: Tree Shaking is a term for dead-code elimination in JavaScript bundlers (Webpack, Rollup). Static analysis of ES Module `import`/`export` statements enables bundlers to detect and remove un-referenced exports from final production bundles.
keyTakeaways: Eliminates dead, unused JavaScript code from distribution bundles.
Requires ES Module static structure; fails with dynamic CommonJS `require()`.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why does dynamic `require()` syntax in CommonJS prevent effective tree shaking?
options: Because dynamic module paths cannot be fully resolved prior to runtime execution
Because CJS runs on server environments
Because CJS files lack prototype properties
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Dynamic runtime paths in `require()` prevent static compilers from identifying unused module code safely.

sections.title: Q50 [Coding]: Implement pipe() and compose() functional utilities.
keyTakeaways: `pipe` processes transformations left-to-right via `Array.prototype.reduce()`.
`compose` processes transformations right-to-left via `Array.prototype.reduceRight()`.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the execution order difference between pipe() and compose()?
options: pipe is asynchronous; compose is synchronous
pipe evaluates functions left-to-right; compose evaluates right-to-left
compose works only with arrow functions
interactiveQuiz.explanation: `pipe` chains execution left-to-right, whereas mathematical `compose` evaluates functions right-to-left.

chapters.title: 25 Progressive JavaScript Coding Questions (Easy to Difficult)
chapters.summary: A 25-question coding bank structured from basic JavaScript string/array manipulations to advanced asynchronous control flow, custom polyfills, and engine metaprogramming.

sections.title: Q51: Reverse a String Without Built-In Reverse
sections.content: To reverse a string manually, iterate backward from the last character to the first, appending each character to a new string. This demonstrates basic iteration and string accumulation.
keyTakeaways: Iterates backward from the end of the string to assemble a new reversed string.
Runs with O(n) time complexity and O(n) space complexity.

codeExample.title: Manual String Reversal
codeExample.explanation: By looping from str.length - 1 down to 0, each character is appended in reverse order without using Array.prototype.reverse().

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the time complexity of reversing a string of length n character-by-character?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Visiting each character in a string of length n takes linear time O(n).

sections.title: Q52: Classic FizzBuzz Implementation
sections.content: Output numbers from 1 to N, replacing multiples of 3 with 'Fizz', 5 with 'Buzz', and multiples of both with 'FizzBuzz'. Check compound conditions (multiples of 15) before individual factors.
keyTakeaways: Check for combined conditions (i % 15 === 0) before individual conditions.
Demonstrates basic modulo arithmetic and control flow branching.

codeExample.title: FizzBuzz Loop
codeExample.explanation: Evaluating i % 15 first prevents multiples of both 3 and 5 from matching the earlier single-factor branches.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why must the condition for 15 (or both 3 and 5) be checked first in FizzBuzz?
options: Because modulo operations only work in descending order
Otherwise multiples of 15 would trigger the 3 or 5 branch earlier and skip 'FizzBuzz'
To avoid an out-of-bounds array error
It is optional and makes no difference
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If i % 3 is checked first, numbers like 15 hit the 'Fizz' block and miss 'FizzBuzz'.

sections.title: Q53: Check if a String is a Palindrome
sections.content: Clean non-alphanumeric characters and convert to lower case, then use a two-pointer approach moving toward the center to check if the string reads identically forward and backward.
keyTakeaways: Sanitizes strings using Regular Expressions prior to checking.
Uses a two-pointer approach to compare characters from opposite ends toward the center.

codeExample.title: Two-Pointer Palindrome Validation
codeExample.explanation: Two pointers move inward from opposite ends, allowing early exit as soon as a non-matching character pair is found.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the primary benefit of a two-pointer approach over str === str.split('').reverse().join('')?
options: It runs in O(1) time complexity
It can exit early on the first mismatched pair without processing the entire string
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Two pointers can return false instantly upon finding a character mismatch.

sections.title: Q54: Find Minimum and Maximum Values in an Array
sections.content: Find both min and max values in a single pass across the array without relying on spread syntax with Math.min/Math.max, which can overflow the call stack on large arrays.
keyTakeaways: Performs single-pass O(n) iteration to update bounds.
Avoids Math.max(...arr) which can throw a stack overflow error on very large arrays.

codeExample.title: Single-Pass Min/Max Finder
codeExample.explanation: Iterating once updates min and max tracking variables in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why can Math.max(...largeArray) fail on extremely large arrays (e.g. 100,000+ elements)?
options: Math.max only works on small hardcoded numbers
Exceeds maximum call stack size due to argument spreading
Arrays automatically convert to strings when passed to Math.max
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Spreading massive arrays passes millions of parameters onto the stack frame, triggering a call stack overflow.

sections.title: Q55: Chunk an Array into Sub-Arrays of Fixed Size
sections.content: Split an array into smaller sub-arrays of a target size by iterating through the source array in increments of the chunk size and calling Array.prototype.slice().
keyTakeaways: Advances loop pointer by size steps.
Array.prototype.slice extracts chunks cleanly without mutating the source array.

codeExample.title: Array Chunking Helper
codeExample.explanation: By incrementing the loop index by size each iteration, slice() extracts sub-arrays of exact length.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the result of chunkArray([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Chunks of size 2 extract elements in pairs, leaving the remaining odd element [5] in the final slice.

sections.title: Q56: Count Character Frequencies in a String
sections.content: Count the occurrence of each character in a string by accumulating counts inside a plain object map, initializing unseen characters to zero.
keyTakeaways: Uses logical OR (||) to initialize missing object keys to zero.
Runs in linear O(n) time complexity relative to string length.

codeExample.title: Character Frequency Counter
codeExample.explanation: The expression (freq[char] || 0) ensures that unvisited characters start at 0 before adding 1.

interactiveQuiz.question: What value does freq[char] || 0 evaluate to if char is not yet present in the freq map?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If freq[char] is undefined (falsy), the logical OR falls back to 0.

sections.title: Q57: Remove Duplicate Values from an Array
sections.content: Deduplicate elements in an array using an ES6 Set for linear performance, or Array.prototype.filter() with indexOf() for a single-line functional approach.
keyTakeaways: Set approach provides O(n) time complexity.
filter + indexOf provides O(n²) time complexity due to internal lookup overhead.

codeExample.title: Array Deduplication Approaches
codeExample.explanation: ES6 Set automatically discards duplicate values in linear time, while filter + indexOf scans the array repeatedly.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is the Set approach preferred over filter + indexOf for large arrays?
options: Set takes O(n) linear time, whereas indexOf inside filter takes quadratic O(n²) time
filter converts array elements to strings
filter does not work with numbers
interactiveQuiz.explanation: indexOf executes a full scan per iteration (O(n)), making filter + indexOf O(n²) overall.

sections.title: Q58: Invert Keys and Values of an Object
sections.content: Swap the keys and values of a plain object into a new object using a for...in loop combined with a hasOwnProperty check to ignore prototype properties.
keyTakeaways: Swaps keys and values into a new object.
Uses hasOwnProperty guard to prevent iterating inherited prototype properties.

codeExample.title: Object Key-Value Inversion
codeExample.explanation: Maps each value obj[key] as a key in the new object, assigning the original key string as its value.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens if an object contains multiple duplicate values during inversion (e.g. { a: 1, b: 1 })?
options: Later values overwrite earlier keys under the inverted key target
Converts the value into an array automatically
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Inverted keys are plain object properties; reassigning inverted[1] overwrites prior assignments.

sections.title: Q59: Implement Custom pick and omit Object Helpers
sections.content: Build pick(obj, keys) to extract specific properties into a new object, and omit(obj, keys) to create a copy that excludes specified keys.
keyTakeaways: Reduces object keys dynamically.
Using a Set in omit allows O(1) key exclusion checks.

codeExample.title: Object Pick and Omit Utility
codeExample.explanation: pick filters down to specified keys, while omit uses a Set lookup to drop listed keys efficiently.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the benefit of passing keys as a Set inside the omit function?
options: Ensures keys are converted to numbers
Reduces exclusion lookup complexity from O(k) down to O(1) time per key
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Set.has() performs O(1) lookup checks compared to Array.includes() O(k) linear scans.

sections.title: Q60: Implement Infinite Curried Addition sum(1)(2)(3)...()
sections.content: Create a function that continuously accumulates numbers across chained function calls until called with no arguments to signal termination.
keyTakeaways: Uses closure state to accumulate sum values across chained calls.
Terminates recursive currying when invoked without arguments (b === undefined).

codeExample.title: Infinitely Curried Sum
codeExample.explanation: Each invocation returns a new sum function wrapping the updated total until b === undefined triggers the final total.

interactiveQuiz.question: What acts as the base termination signal for ending the sum currying chain above?
options: Invoking the returned function with no arguments (undefined)
interactiveQuiz.explanation: An empty invocation () passes b = undefined, triggering the return of accumulated sum a.

sections.title: Q61: Implement Promise Timeout (Cancel Race)
sections.content: Wrap a target Promise with a timeout reject mechanism using Promise.race, ensuring the operation fails if it exceeds a specified delay threshold.
keyTakeaways: Promise.race resolves or rejects as soon as any promise in the array settles.
Combines target promise against a timer reject promise.

codeExample.title: Promise Timeout Wrapper
codeExample.explanation: Promise.race resolves with the target result if it completes before the setTimeout reject fires.

interactiveQuiz.question: If the main promise resolves in 500ms and the timeout is set to 1000ms, what is the output of Promise.race?
options: Resolves with the value from the main promise
Returns both settled values in an array
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Because 500ms < 1000ms, the main promise settles first and wins the Promise.race.

sections.title: Q62: Write a Custom Function.prototype.bind Polyfill
sections.content: Implement a custom version of Function.prototype.bind that captures context and initial bound arguments, returning a function that accepts additional arguments at call time.
keyTakeaways: Captures this target function inside a closure.
Concatenates initial boundArgs with execution call args during invocation.

codeExample.title: Function bind Polyfill
codeExample.explanation: myBind returns a wrapper that applies the stored context and combines initial boundArgs with invocation arguments.

interactiveQuiz.question: How are initial arguments passed to myBind merged with arguments passed to the bound execution function?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Partial application combines initial bound arguments with secondary execution arguments sequentially.

sections.title: Q63: Write a URL Query String Parser and Builder
sections.content: Implement helper functions to convert URL query parameters into an object map and convert an object map back into an encoded URL query string.
keyTakeaways: Processes delimiter split strings using split('&') and split('=').
Encodes and decodes special URI characters using encodeURIComponent and decodeURIComponent.

codeExample.title: Query Parser and Stringifier
codeExample.explanation: Splitting by delimiters extracts key-value pairs while URI encoding functions prevent character corruption.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why must encodeURIComponent be used when stringifying query parameters?
options: To convert objects into JSON strings
To escape reserved URL characters like &, =, ?, and spaces safely
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Unescaped reserved characters inside parameter values corrupt URL parameter parsing delimiters.

sections.title: Q64: Implement an Async Publish-Subscribe Bus
sections.content: Create an event bus that supports asynchronous subscriber callbacks, returning a promise from publish() that resolves once all subscriber callbacks settle.
keyTakeaways: Returns an un-subscribe teardown closure upon registration.
Uses Promise.all to execute and await subscriber handlers concurrently during publication.

codeExample.title: Async Event Bus
codeExample.explanation: Publishing wraps each callback in a Promise, allowing Promise.all to await all subscriber operations concurrently.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the return result of publishing an event in the AsyncEventBus above?
options: A Promise resolving to an array of output results from all subscriber callbacks
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Promise.all returns a promise resolving to an array containing outcomes of subscriber callbacks.

sections.title: Q65: Write a Simple Virtual DOM Render Function
sections.content: Implement a render(vnode) function that converts Virtual DOM element objects ({ type, props, children }) or text primitives into real DOM Node instances.
keyTakeaways: Recursively processes tree node structures using DOM API creation calls.
Distinguishes text nodes, attribute props, and on event listener bindings.

codeExample.title: VNode to Real DOM Compiler
codeExample.explanation: Recursively converts element descriptors into real DOM nodes, registering event listeners for 'on' props.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does the render function handle event props like onClick: fn?
options: Strips the 'on' prefix and attaches an event listener via addEventListener('click', fn)
Evaluates the function as inline script string
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Prop names starting with on are sliced (onClick -> click) and registered using addEventListener.

sections.title: Q66: Implement an Async Waterfall Sequencer
sections.content: Build an async pipeline helper that executes an array of asynchronous functions sequentially, passing the output of each function as input to the next.
keyTakeaways: Chains Promise resolution steps sequentially using Array.prototype.reduce.
Executes asynchronous pipeline processing, passing forward computed outcomes.

codeExample.title: Sequential Async Pipeline
codeExample.explanation: Array.reduce builds a continuous Promise chain where each task executes only after the previous task resolves.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does asyncWaterfall guarantee sequential execution over concurrent Promise.all execution?
options: By chaining .then() calls onto a single Promise reduce accumulator
By running code inside a while loop
By sorting tasks by execution speed
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Chaining .then() delegates next task execution until previous task promises settle.

sections.title: Q67: Implement Deep Freeze for Complete Immutability
sections.content: Extend Object.freeze() to recursively freeze all nested object and array properties to guarantee complete object graph immutability.
keyTakeaways: Native Object.freeze() is shallow and does not freeze nested object properties.
Recursively freezes child objects to guarantee deep immutability.

codeExample.title: Recursive Deep Freeze
codeExample.explanation: Deep freeze invokes Object.freeze() at the current level, then recursively traverses and freezes all nested object properties.

interactiveQuiz.question: What occurs when attempting to mutate a property on a deepFrozen object in strict mode?
options: Throws a TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property
Mutates property temporarily until page refresh
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Mutating frozen object properties in strict mode raises an explicit TypeError.

sections.title: Q68: Implement a Time and Size Batch Request Scheduler
sections.content: Build a batcher that accumulates incoming items and flushes them to a processing handler whenever maximum batch size is reached OR maximum delay time elapses.
keyTakeaways: Dual trigger batching: flushes immediately on max size or automatically on timer expiration.
Optimizes network requests by combining multiple individual calls into single batch payload calls.

codeExample.title: Batch Request Scheduler
codeExample.explanation: Reaching maxSize triggers an immediate flush; otherwise a timer schedules a flush after maxDelay.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is the timer cleared inside flush() during max size execution triggers?
options: To prevent a duplicate flush of empty or partial batches when the timer elapses later
Because setTimeout functions are limited to one execution
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If max size triggers a flush early, clearing timer prevents firing duplicate empty flushes.

sections.title: Q69: Calculate Structural Difference Between Two Objects
sections.content: Implement diffObjects(obj1, obj2) to compare two objects recursively and return a summary of added, removed, and updated properties.
keyTakeaways: Combines key sets to evaluate deletions, additions, and mutations.
Recursively evaluates nested object structures to identify structural changes.

codeExample.title: Object Diffing Utility
codeExample.explanation: Collects keys across both objects to determine property additions, removals, and value mutations recursively.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does the diffObjects algorithm identify a key that was REMOVED in obj2?
options: key in obj1 is true, but key in obj2 is false
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Checking property presence (!(key in obj2)) identifies keys present in the source object but missing in target.

sections.title: Q70: Create a Reactive Auto-Tracking State Store Using Proxy
sections.content: Create an automated reactive store where accessing properties inside a watchEffect callback registers dependencies and mutating properties triggers re-execution.
keyTakeaways: Core architecture powering reactivity in modern frameworks (e.g. Vue 3 Reactivity).
get traps track active effect dependencies; set traps notify and re-run dependent effects.

codeExample.title: Proxy-Based Reactive State Store
codeExample.explanation: Active effects trigger getter traps to register keys as dependencies, allowing setter traps to re-run affected callbacks on change.

interactiveQuiz.question: How does watchEffect automatically detect which store keys an effect function depends on?
options: By parsing the function code string with Regex
By setting activeEffect and executing the function, causing getters on used state properties to record the dependency
By requiring hardcoded key lists from developers
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Executing the effect function triggers get proxy traps on accessed properties, registering dependencies automatically.

sections.title: Q71: Implement Custom myInstanceOf Operator
sections.content: Replicate the behavior of the instanceof operator by traversing the prototype chain of an object to check for matching constructor prototypes.
keyTakeaways: Traverses Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) upward step by step.
Returns true if target constructor.prototype is found anywhere along the prototype chain.

codeExample.title: Custom instanceof Implementation
codeExample.explanation: Walks Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) upward until finding constructor.prototype or reaching the null prototype root.

interactiveQuiz.question: What value does Object.getPrototypeOf() return when called at the top termination point of the prototype chain?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Object.prototype.__proto__ evaluates to null, signaling the end of prototype chain traversal.

sections.title: Q72: Implement Custom Promise.allSettled Polyfill
sections.content: Polyfill Promise.allSettled using Promise.all by wrapping individual inner promises so rejections resolve into structured result objects.
keyTakeaways: Wraps each inner promise in .then() and .catch() blocks that map settlement to objects.
Leverages Promise.all over mapped promises since wrapped promises never reject.

codeExample.title: Promise.allSettled Polyfill
codeExample.explanation: Handling rejections inside inner .catch() blocks ensures Promise.all receives only resolved outcome descriptors.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why does myPromiseAllSettled wrapping allow Promise.all to resolve without rejecting early?
options: Because inner .catch() handlers convert rejections into resolved fulfillment objects
Because rejection values are converted to 0
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Handling errors inside inner .catch() calls returns a resolved object, keeping Promise.all from rejecting.

sections.title: Q73: Build a Basic Virtual DOM Tree Diffing Engine
sections.content: Build a diffing engine that compares old and new Virtual DOM node trees recursively, generating patch descriptions for updates, replacements, and removals.
keyTakeaways: Compares VNodes recursively to calculate minimal structural edits.
Replaces entire subtrees when VNode type tags differ.

codeExample.title: VNode Diffing Algorithm
codeExample.explanation: Compares VNodes recursively, returning REPLACE patches when tag types change or UPDATE patches for modified props/children.

interactiveQuiz.question: What patch action is returned when comparing two VNodes with different element type tags (e.g. div vs section)?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Mismatched element types signal that the subtree cannot be updated in-place and must be completely replaced.

sections.title: Q74: Build a Priority-Based Asynchronous Job Queue
sections.content: Implement an asynchronous job queue that sorts queued tasks by numeric priority values so higher priority jobs execute first under concurrency limits.
keyTakeaways: Orders pending tasks by priority before processing.
Enforces concurrency limits while processing high-priority tasks first.

codeExample.title: Priority Async Queue
codeExample.explanation: Tasks are sorted by priority score upon insertion, ensuring highest-priority items shift out first when worker slots open.

interactiveQuiz.question: In what order are pending tasks processed by the PriorityAsyncQueue above?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Sorting by b.priority - a.priority ensures high-priority jobs shift out of the queue first.

sections.title: Q75: Build a Custom Stream Transform Pipeline Component
sections.content: Create a data stream processor that processes stream chunks sequentially through composed async transform middleware, allowing chunks to be modified or filtered out.
keyTakeaways: Pipes individual stream chunks through sequentially composed transformation middleware.
Supports filtering chunks from the stream when transform functions return null or undefined.

codeExample.title: Transform Stream Pipeline
codeExample.explanation: Applies sequential transforms to each chunk. Returning null inside any transform halts the middleware chain and drops the chunk.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens when a transformation function in the pipeline returns null for a specific chunk?
options: The chunk is skipped and discarded from remaining transformations and final results
Null is appended to the results array
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Returning null signals a filter step, breaking the transformation loop for that chunk and skipping emission.

chapters.title: 25 Essential Data Structures & Algorithms Coding Questions
chapters.summary: A 25-question DSA problem bank covering arrays, strings, linked lists, trees, graphs, dynamic programming, and algorithm paradigms using the codeExample format.

sections.title: Q1: Two Sum
sections.content: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`. Use a Hash Map to reduce lookup complexity to O(1).
keyTakeaways: Hash Map provides O(n) time complexity by storing complement values during iteration.
Avoids the naive O(n²) nested loop approach.

codeExample.title: Hash Map Two Sum Solution
codeExample.explanation: As we iterate through nums, we calculate the complement required to reach target. If the complement exists in our map, we immediately return its stored index and the current index.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the time and space complexity of the Hash Map solution for Two Sum?
options: O(n log n) time and O(n) space
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Iterating the array takes O(n) time, and storing elements in a map takes O(n) auxiliary space.

sections.title: Q2: Valid Parentheses
sections.content: Given a string containing `()`, `{}`, and `[]`, determine if the input string is valid using a Stack data structure.
keyTakeaways: Stacks enforce Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) tracking for nested structure validations.
The string is invalid if an unexpected closing bracket appears or if brackets remain on the stack at the end.

codeExample.title: Stack Parentheses Validator
codeExample.explanation: Opening brackets are pushed onto the stack. When a closing bracket is encountered, we pop the stack and verify that it matches the corresponding opening bracket type.

interactiveQuiz.question: What condition indicates an unclosed opening bracket after processing the entire string?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If opening brackets were pushed but never matched with a closing bracket, the stack remains non-empty.

sections.title: Q3: Reverse a Singly Linked List
sections.content: Reverse a singly linked list in-place by reassigning the `next` pointers using three iteration references: `prev`, `curr`, and `next`.
keyTakeaways: Reverses pointers in linear O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
Requires storing `curr.next` in a temporary pointer before updating node link.

codeExample.title: Iterative Linked List Reversal
codeExample.explanation: At each step, we save curr.next, point curr.next backward to prev, advance prev to curr, and move curr to the saved nextTemp pointer.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which reference becomes the new head of the reversed linked list upon loop completion?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: When `curr` reaches `null`, `prev` points to the last processed node, which is the new head of the reversed list.

sections.title: Q4: Merge Two Sorted Lists
sections.content: Merge two sorted linked lists into one single sorted list by creating a dummy node and chaining smaller node values iteratively.
keyTakeaways: A dummy head node simplifies boundary edge cases when building the merged list.
Runs in O(n + m) time complexity where n and m are lengths of the lists.

codeExample.title: Sorted List Merge
codeExample.explanation: Compares front nodes of both lists, attaches the smaller node to tail, and advances that list's pointer. Any remaining nodes are appended at the end.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is a dummy node used at the start of the algorithm?
options: To avoid special-case conditionals when initializing the new head pointer
To make linked list nodes contiguous in V8 memory
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Using a dummy node avoids writing separate initial-assignment branches to establish the head pointer.

sections.title: Q5: Binary Search
sections.content: Search for a target value within a sorted array using the divide-and-conquer strategy, reducing the search space by half in each iteration.
keyTakeaways: Requires a sorted array input.
Achieves logarithmic O(log n) time complexity.

codeExample.title: Binary Search Implementation
codeExample.explanation: Calculates mid index safely. If target is larger than nums[mid], discards the left half; otherwise discards the right half.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is Math.floor(left + (right - left) / 2) preferred over Math.floor((left + right) / 2)?
options: Prevents potential integer overflow issues in languages with fixed integer limits when left and right are very large
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Adding large bounds `(left + right)` directly can exceed max safe integer bounds in fixed 32-bit systems.

sections.title: Q6: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm)
sections.content: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum within an array of numbers using Kadane's dynamic programming algorithm.
keyTakeaways: Kadane's algorithm runs in linear O(n) time complexity with O(1) space.
At each element, decides whether to extend the current sum or start a new subarray sum.

codeExample.title: Kadane's Algorithm Solution
codeExample.explanation: currentSum updates to either the current item alone or current item plus previous running sum, whichever is greater, while maxSum tracks global maximum.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the time complexity of Kadane's Algorithm?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Kadane's Algorithm scans the array in a single pass taking O(n) linear time.

sections.title: Q7: Linked List Cycle Detection (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare)
sections.content: Detect whether a linked list contains a cycle using two pointers moving at different speeds (slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps).
keyTakeaways: Floyd's algorithm detects cycles in O(n) time and O(1) space.
If a cycle exists, the fast pointer eventually catches up and equals the slow pointer.

codeExample.title: Floyd's Cycle Finding Algorithm
codeExample.explanation: Slow moves one node at a time while fast moves two nodes. If there is no cycle, fast reaches null. If a cycle exists, fast meets slow inside the loop.

interactiveQuiz.question: What happens if Floyd's cycle detection is run on a linear list with no cycle?
options: fast pointer reaches null and function returns false
interactiveQuiz.explanation: When no cycle exists, `fast` or `fast.next` hits `null`, breaking the loop cleanly.

sections.title: Q8: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
sections.content: Find the maximum profit possible from buying stock on one day and selling it on a future day given an array of daily stock prices.
keyTakeaways: Single pass algorithm maintaining lowest price seen so far.
Achieves O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space complexity.

codeExample.title: Max Profit Calculator
codeExample.explanation: Tracks minPrice encountered up to the current day. Max profit is updated if selling today yields higher profit than previously recorded maximum.

interactiveQuiz.question: What profit is returned if stock prices strictly decrease continuously (e.g. [7, 6, 4, 3, 1])?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If no profitable transaction can be made, `maxProfit` remains initialized at `0`.

sections.title: Q9: Invert Binary Tree
sections.content: Invert or mirror a binary tree recursively by swapping left and right child pointers for every node in the tree.
keyTakeaways: Uses Depth-First Search (DFS) tree recursion.
Swaps `.left` and `.right` pointers at every level.

codeExample.title: Recursive Binary Tree Inversion
codeExample.explanation: Base case returns null. At each node, its left child receives the inverted right subtree and its right child receives the inverted left subtree.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the time complexity of inverting a binary tree with N nodes?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Every node in the tree must be visited once, taking linear O(N) time.

sections.title: Q10: Valid Anagram
sections.content: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s` (contains exact same character frequencies).
keyTakeaways: Return false early if string lengths differ.
Use a single frequency map or fixed 26-character array to count frequencies.

codeExample.title: Frequency Map Anagram Check
codeExample.explanation: Increments character counts for string `s` and decrements for string `t`. If a character in `t` has zero count or doesn't exist, strings are not anagrams.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the space complexity if solving anagram verification using frequency map over ASCII/lowercase letters?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Since the alphabet size is bounded (e.g. 26 lower-case letters), frequency map space complexity is constant O(1).

sections.title: Q11: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
sections.content: Calculate the maximum depth (number of nodes along the longest path from root to leaf) of a binary tree recursively.
keyTakeaways: Depth equals `1 + max(depth(left), depth(right))`.
Base case for null nodes returns depth 0.

codeExample.title: Tree Maximum Depth (DFS)
codeExample.explanation: Recursively measures the depth of left and right child subtrees and returns the greater depth plus 1 for the current root node.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the worst-case space complexity of recursive maxDepth on a completely skewed tree?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: In a completely unbalanced skewed tree (linked list structure), the call stack depth reaches O(N).

sections.title: Q12: Container With Most Water
sections.content: Given $n$ non-negative integers representing vertical lines, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container holding the maximum water.
keyTakeaways: Two-pointer approach moving inward from left and right edges.
Always advance the pointer holding the shorter height to search for larger area candidates.

codeExample.title: Two-Pointer Container Area Maximizer
codeExample.explanation: Calculates container area bounded by shorter line. Advances shorter boundary pointer inward since moving the taller pointer could never increase height area.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is the shorter pointer moved inward in each iteration step?
options: Because keeping the shorter line limits maximum area while width decreases
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Width decreases as pointers move inward; the only way to increase area is by finding a taller limiting line.

sections.title: Q13: 3Sum Problem
sections.content: Find all unique triplets in an array that sum to zero using sorting and two pointers.
keyTakeaways: Sort array first to enable two-pointer traversal and duplicate skipping.
Runs in O(n²) time complexity.

codeExample.title: Sorted Two-Pointer 3Sum
codeExample.explanation: Fixes item i and solves Two Sum for -nums[i] on the remaining sorted sub-array, skipping duplicate elements to ensure unique triplets.

interactiveQuiz.question: What step prevents returning duplicate triplet sets in the output array?
options: Skipping identical neighboring elements after sorting
Converting output array to a JSON string
Sorting the array in descending order
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Because the array is sorted, identical adjacent values can be skipped using `while` conditionals.

sections.title: Q14: Climbing Stairs (Dynamic Programming)
sections.content: You are climbing a staircase requiring $n$ steps. Each time you can climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?
keyTakeaways: Follows Fibonacci sequence progression: $dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]$.
Can be solved in O(n) time and O(1) space using dynamic programming space optimization.

codeExample.title: DP Climbing Stairs Solution
codeExample.explanation: To reach step i, you can arrive from step i-1 or step i-2. Summing these options gives total ways, matching Fibonacci transitions.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the space complexity of the variable-tracking dynamic programming approach above?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Tracking only the previous two step values requires constant O(1) auxiliary space.

sections.title: Q15: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
sections.content: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters using the Sliding Window pattern.
keyTakeaways: Sliding window uses two pointers (`left`, `right`) and a Set/Map.
Achieves O(n) linear time complexity.

codeExample.title: Sliding Window Substring Search
codeExample.explanation: Right pointer expands window. When duplicate character is detected, left pointer contracts window until duplicate is removed from set.

interactiveQuiz.question: What triggers the left window pointer to contract inward?
options: Detecting a character already present inside the active seen set
Reaching the middle of the string
interactiveQuiz.explanation: When `s[right]` is inside `seen`, `left` increments and removes characters until uniqueness is restored.

sections.title: Q16: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (BFS)
sections.content: Perform level-order traversal on a binary tree using a Queue (Breadth-First Search) returning nodes grouped level by level.
keyTakeaways: Breadth-First Search (BFS) processes nodes level by level using a queue.
Tracks level size (`queue.length`) at loop start to process nodes layer by layer.

codeExample.title: BFS Level Order Traversal
codeExample.explanation: Queue processes nodes layer by layer. The inner loop iterates `levelSize` times to group current level values into a separate output subarray.

interactiveQuiz.question: Which data structure is fundamentally required for Breadth-First Search (BFS)?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: BFS relies on First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue ordering to process shallower nodes before deeper nodes.

sections.title: Q17: Coin Change (Dynamic Programming)
sections.content: Find the minimum number of coins needed to make up a given amount using bottom-up dynamic programming.
keyTakeaways: Dynamic Programming lookup table array initialized to `Infinity`.
State transition: `dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1)`.

codeExample.title: Bottom-Up DP Coin Change
codeExample.explanation: dp[i] stores min coins needed for amount i. Iterates through all available coins to find minimum coin combinations step by step.

interactiveQuiz.question: What value does coinChange return if the target amount cannot be made by any coin combination?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If `dp[amount]` remains `Infinity` after loop evaluation, the function returns `-1`.

sections.title: Q18: Validate Binary Search Tree
sections.content: Determine if a given binary tree is a valid Binary Search Tree (BST) where left subtree values are strictly smaller and right subtree values are strictly larger than root.
keyTakeaways: Pass lower and upper boundary bounds recursively during DFS traversal.
Checking only immediate child nodes is insufficient; subtrees must satisfy full boundary limits.

codeExample.title: BST Boundary Range Validation
codeExample.explanation: Validates node value against allowable min and max constraints. When stepping left, updates max bound to current node value; when stepping right, updates min bound.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is checking if root.left.val < root.val and root.right.val > root.val insufficient for verifying a BST?
options: Deeper nodes in a right subtree could violate root constraints while being valid relative to their immediate parent
Binary Search Trees allow duplicate values anywhere
interactiveQuiz.explanation: All nodes in a right subtree must be greater than the ancestor root node, not just the immediate child.

sections.title: Q19: Number of Islands (Graph DFS/BFS)
sections.content: Count the number of distinct islands in a 2D grid of `'1'`s (land) and `'0'`s (water) using Depth-First Search (DFS).
keyTakeaways: Treat grid as an undirected graph and sink visited land nodes by mutating `'1'` to `'0'`.
Increments island count on finding an unvisited `'1'` and triggers flood-fill DFS.

codeExample.title: Grid DFS Flood Fill Island Counter
codeExample.explanation: Scans every cell. When encountering land ('1'), increments island count and starts DFS flood-fill to mark all connected land cells as visited ('0').

interactiveQuiz.question: Why does the DFS function mutate grid[r][c] = '0' during flood fill?
options: To sink visited land so it is not re-counted as a separate island later
Because 0 values represent higher priority land
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Mutating visited land cells to `'0'` acts as a visited tracking set without allocating auxiliary memory.

sections.title: Q20: Kth Largest Element in an Array
sections.content: Find the $k$-th largest element in an unsorted array using QuickSelect partitioning algorithm or Min-Heap.
keyTakeaways: QuickSelect provides average O(n) time complexity.
Avoids full array sorting which takes O(n log n).

codeExample.title: QuickSelect Partition Algorithm
codeExample.explanation: Partitions array around pivot. If pivot index equals target position (length - k), returns target value; otherwise selectively recurses into the target partition half.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the average time complexity of QuickSelect?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: By discarding half of the partition search space each step ($n + n/2 + n/4...$), QuickSelect achieves O(n) average time.

sections.title: Q21: Course Schedule (Topological Sort / Cycle Detection)
sections.content: Determine if you can finish all courses given prerequisite pairs using Topological Sort / Kahn's Algorithm (In-degree array + BFS).
keyTakeaways: If a directed graph contains a cycle, topological sorting is impossible.
Kahn's algorithm tracks in-degrees of nodes to identify valid task processing order.

codeExample.title: Kahn's Algorithm BFS Topological Sort
codeExample.explanation: Calculates in-degree counts for each node. Courses with 0 prerequisites enter the BFS queue. Decrements in-degrees of dependent courses as completed; returns true if all courses can be processed.

interactiveQuiz.question: What condition indicates that prerequisites contain a cyclic dependency loop?
options: processedCount is less than total numCourses
interactiveQuiz.explanation: If a cycle exists, cyclic nodes never reach in-degree 0, leaving `processedCount < numCourses`.

sections.title: Q22: Word Search (Backtracking)
sections.content: Determine if a target word exists in a 2D board of letters by constructing adjacent character paths using Backtracking DFS.
keyTakeaways: Backtracking recursively explores possibilities and reverts choice state upon reaching dead ends.
Temporarily mark board cells (e.g. `'#'`) during exploration to prevent self-revisiting.

codeExample.title: 2D Grid Backtracking Search
codeExample.explanation: Explores neighbors recursively if character matches word[index]. Restores cell state (board[r][c] = temp) when returning so other path branches can reuse the cell.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why must board[r][c] be restored back to its original character value before returning from backtrack()?
options: To allow other valid search path explorations to reuse the cell
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Restoring state during backtracking ensures failed paths leave the grid unchanged for future search paths.

sections.title: Q23: Merge K Sorted Lists
sections.content: Merge $k$ sorted linked lists into one consolidated sorted list using Divide and Conquer or Min-Heap.
keyTakeaways: Divide and conquer merges pairs of lists iteratively.
Reduces time complexity to O(N log k) where N is total node count across k lists.

codeExample.title: Divide and Conquer List Merger
codeExample.explanation: Pairs up lists and merges each pair using mergeTwoLists, halving the total number of lists each pass until only one sorted list remains.

interactiveQuiz.question: What is the time complexity of merging K sorted lists with total N nodes using Divide and Conquer?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Halving $k$ lists takes $\log k$ pair-merge passes, with each pass processing $N$ total nodes.

sections.title: Q24: Trapping Rain Water
sections.content: Calculate how much water an elevation map can trap after raining using Two Pointers.
keyTakeaways: Water trapped at any position is bounded by $\min(\text{maxLeft}, \text{maxRight}) - \text{height}[i]$.
Two pointers allow tracking boundary bounds in O(n) time and O(1) space.

codeExample.title: Two-Pointer Water Trapping
codeExample.explanation: Maintains leftMax and rightMax bounds. Advances shorter pointer inward and adds trapped water based on difference between local max bound and bar height.

interactiveQuiz.question: What determines the water level trapped above height[left] when height[left] < height[right]?
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Because `height[left] < height[right]`, we know `rightMax` is at least equal to `height[right]`, so `leftMax` acts as the limiting boundary wall.

sections.title: Q25: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
sections.content: Find the median of two sorted arrays `nums1` and `nums2` in O(log(min(m, n))) time complexity using Binary Search partitioning.
keyTakeaways: Applies Binary Search on the smaller array to find a valid partition point.
Valid partition occurs when `maxLeftA <= minRightB` and `maxLeftB <= minRightA`.

codeExample.title: Binary Search Partition Median Finder
codeExample.explanation: Executes binary search on smaller array nums1 to find partition splits where left halves elements are smaller than right halves elements, giving median in O(log(min(m, n))) time.

interactiveQuiz.question: Why is Binary Search performed specifically on the smaller of the two input arrays?
options: Minimizes search range bounds to guarantee O(log(min(m, n))) time complexity
Prevents array index out of bounds exceptions
Required because small arrays contain lower numbers
interactiveQuiz.explanation: Binary searching the smaller array minimizes total search operations to logarithmic time relative to the smaller length `min(m, n)`.
